test.title: Counting the trees in a city

texts.title: Counting the trees in a city

paragraphs.text: A city that does not know how many trees it owns cannot plan for them, and until recently almost none did. Street trees were planted by whoever was in charge at the time, recorded on paper that was lost in the next reorganisation, and remembered only when one fell on a car. The first inventories were made not out of curiosity but out of liability: insurers began asking councils to show that their trees were inspected, and an inspection regime needs a list. What began as a defence against claims has turned into the main source of evidence in every argument a city now has about its trees.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Making the list is more work than it sounds. A surveyor walking a street records the species, the diameter of the trunk at chest height, the height, the condition of the crown, the space available for roots and the nearest building, and fixes the position on a map to within a metre. A trained pair can do perhaps two hundred trees a day in an easy suburb and half that where cars are parked bumper to bumper. For a city with a quarter of a million street trees, the first survey is a project of several years. The second is far cheaper, because the hard part is not measuring a tree but finding it, and a tree found once stays found.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Aerial and satellite data reduce the walking but do not replace it. Laser scanning from aircraft gives height and crown volume across a whole city in a few flights, and repeat scans show growth and loss; what they cannot give is species below the canopy, the condition of the trunk, or whether the roots have room. The practical arrangement in most cities is a scan that covers everything and a walking survey of the streets, with the two datasets joined by position. Neither on its own answers the questions a city actually asks, which are about risk, shade and what to plant next.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The numbers that come out are used to argue for money, and here the arithmetic needs care. A mature tree in a street intercepts rainfall, shades asphalt, filters particles and takes up a measurable quantity of carbon, and several widely used tools convert these into an annual value in currency. The figures are useful for comparison between streets and are treated with suspicion by economists when they are added up into a headline total, because the assumptions inside them were calibrated on a handful of North American cities.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: What the inventories reveal most consistently is inequality. In city after city, the tree canopy is thickest in the wealthiest districts and thinnest in the poorest, and the difference is often a factor of three or four. The history behind this is not mysterious: the poorer districts were built at higher density with narrower pavements, were less often planted, and lost what they had to road widening. The consequence is measurable in summer, when the difference in air temperature between a shaded street and a bare one a kilometre away can reach several degrees. Since heat kills the old and the ill before it inconveniences anyone else, the map of the canopy turns out to be a map of something else as well.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A list also changes how trees are managed. Where records exist, inspection moves from complaint-driven to cyclical, pruning is planned rather than emergency, and the species mix can be steered away from monocultures, which matter because a single disease can remove a quarter of a city’s canopy in a decade. Cities that have been through such a loss plant to a rule of thumb — no more than ten per cent of one species, twenty per cent of one genus, thirty per cent of one family — which is easy to state and hard to follow in a nursery trade that grows what sells.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The uncomfortable finding is about survival. Newly planted street trees die at rates that surprise the public and not the people planting them: a fifth in the first three years is normal in a hard site, and the commonest causes are not vandalism but drought in the first two summers and a pit that is too small for the roots. Cities that pay for three years of watering after planting lose fewer trees than cities that plant twice as many and walk away, which is a dull conclusion and the one the data keeps producing.
paragraphs.label: G
